title: The Wardens of Dawn and Dusk

chapters.title: The Wardens of Dawn and Dusk

paras.text:
THE
WARDENS OF DAWN AND DUSK
paras.html: THE WARDENS OF DAWN AND DUSK

paras.text: A Comparative Account

From the Proceedings of the
Archival Committee, Citadel Repository of Letters, CP 1019. Prepared by the Office of
Textual Curation, with the Department of Ancient and Common Imperial Languages, occasioned by three
recoveries of the present cycle.
paras.html: From the Proceedings of the Archival Committee, Citadel Repository of Letters, CP 1019. Prepared by the Office of Textual Curation, with the Department of Ancient and Common Imperial Languages, occasioned by three recoveries of the present cycle.

paras.text:
It is the pleasure of the
Committee, whenever possible, to enlarge the public understanding of the
institutions that shaped our first era. Presently we concern ourselves with the
Dawnwarden Corps and the Duskwarden Order, both of which still exist today in
reformed capacity. But one must wonder the extent of their metamorphosis in the
course of a thousand years. Several documents have recently come into the
Repository’s keeping, and together they shine new light.

We begin with the order better
known to us, and dearer.

THE
DAWNWARDEN CORPS

We often imagine the golden
company to be a ceremonial body, but this was not always the case: they were
the foremost martial order of the empire, drawn from its most able. The state
processions we enjoy today are only a glimpse of their original function.

While the Dämmerung Era was
primordial in its formation, those newly gathered under the Dawn required more
than safety. It required a pride in that assurance, drawing upon the best
toward its service rather than against it, and forging bond between the throne
and those it governed. The Dawnwarden Corps was this noble emissary, given
face.

Chief among the dawnwarden
charges was the Eternal Flame of the Prytaneion (always kept by a standing
detail of twelve). To stand the flame-watch was the highest honor, the ceasing
of this flame utterly unthinkable.

If there is any doubt in the
prowess of the Corps, one need only revisit the Samarkand Accord in CP 544,
when Khan Toghan rose among the northern steppes to unite the clans of his
homeland. In response, the Crown dispatched Captain Hannibal Demaria to the
khan’s court as an imperial envoy. Records suggest a friendship developed
between the two men, and during this time the khan’s confederation did not
further encroach against imperial territory.

The Accord ended where it
began. Khan Toghan ordered Samarkand burned in response to an unknown
provocation. Captain Demaria was unable to dissuade him in private counsel, and
drew his blade to protect thousands of lives. It was here he smote the great khan,
though he would also die in the process.

His sacrifice felled the rising
threat that single afternoon. Having lost its unifying figure, the tribes of
Ashokan returned to isolation and self-governance under the loose overlordship
of the khan’s half-brother. The people of Samarkand maintained independence as
a protectorate of the empire until they were officially reabsorbed in CP 902.

This brave dawnwarden lies in
an honored sepulcher in the necropolis of Gur-e-Amir, watched over by the
figure of a small peregrine.

A Letter from Captain
Hannibal Demaria to the Khan Toghan. Dated 23rd of the Star, CP
544, bequeathed to the Crown from the Ashokan Khanate as a gesture of peace and
goodwill.
paras.html: A Letter from Captain Hannibal Demaria to the Khan Toghan. Dated 23rd of the Star, CP 544, bequeathed to the Crown from the Ashokan Khanate as a gesture of peace and goodwill.

Helena sends her warmth from our father’s
house, wishing you a prosperous new cycle. I must prepare you, for over the
winter she set about a composition of steppe philosophies, and now seeks your
indulgence. Rather fervently, I might add.

enthusiasm, I’ve nonetheless been tasked with a presentation of the manuscript

A merchant of Kashgar told me, in his cup, that he’d been strongarmed into

paras.text:
It is the general consensus
that Khulan was a peregrine gifted to Hannibal in the course of their
fellowship. The memoirs of the khan’s half-brother support this, describing a
falconry tradition of speaking with peregrines through the ritual consumption
of ayahuasca, a psychedelic capable of inducing heightened emotional awareness.
He records that his brother the khan “taught the practice to the messenger
before their fracture.”

THE
DUSKWARDEN ORDER

While equally known, much of
their purpose has been shrouded in mystery. Their official role held them to be
a counterintelligence service charged with the management of sedition. This is
the account preserved in civic history, but the recovery of the earliest known
Duskwarden Charter causes us to rethink the particulars.

It is a single tablet found
within the depths of Citadel’s catacombs, strictly translated here into
Imperial Common. We caution the reader that it does not suggest the function of
a counterintelligence bureau.

The Charter of the
Duskwarden Order

I. The Dawn must rise upon a quiet world. So the citizen may wake
to harmony and never learn its price, our family keeps the night. We do not
begrudge the morning its peace, nor fault our brothers for their ease. The
duskwarden who pursues his own vanity condemns himself to the gloam.
paras.html: I. The Dawn must rise upon a quiet world. So the citizen may wake to harmony and never learn its price, our family keeps the night. We do not begrudge the morning its peace, nor fault our brothers for their ease. The duskwarden who pursues his own vanity condemns himself to the gloam.

paras.text:
II. Truth guides the hand. Wherever hearts are given to rebellion,
accounts may be settled. To settle a debt you cannot enumerate is theft, for
you have taken what the Dawn has not called due. Without exception, the warden
errs toward morning.
paras.html: II. Truth guides the hand. Wherever hearts are given to rebellion, accounts may be settled. To settle a debt you cannot enumerate is theft, for you have taken what the Dawn has not called due. Without exception, the warden errs toward morning.

paras.text:
III. The warden rules his undertow. The cruel are carried toward
the deed, the gentle away from it, and neither has willed a thing. Let the
warden stand in his current, and let him not move a step he did not choose.
paras.html: III. The warden rules his undertow. The cruel are carried toward the deed, the gentle away from it, and neither has willed a thing. Let the warden stand in his current, and let him not move a step he did not choose.

paras.text:
IV. A knight of the dusk sharpens himself for the gloam that would
find him unprepared. Will without strength is death, and the morning shall be
brighter for your absence.
paras.html: IV. A knight of the dusk sharpens himself for the gloam that would find him unprepared. Will without strength is death, and the morning shall be brighter for your absence.

paras.text:
V. The watch is not set down. The warden who dies in service to
the Dawn is welcomed into Dusk itself. He who breaks his oath embraces the
gloam he was sworn to end. Him the family does not mourn, but settles, and
hunts home.
paras.html: V. The watch is not set down. The warden who dies in service to the Dawn is welcomed into Dusk itself. He who breaks his oath embraces the gloam he was sworn to end. Him the family does not mourn, but settles, and hunts home.

paras.text:
The reader will have noted the
same as our team, in what the language implies.

On the First Tenet. The
Order understood itself and the dawnwardens as two branches of one tree. “We do
not begrudge the morning its forgetting” is thus a vow, and to go unthanked was
the accepted price of the work. Note that dusk was a righteous dark the warden
kept on the morning’s behalf; gloam was its corruption. The duskwarden served
the one and destroyed the other.

On the Second Tenet. This
Tenet defines restraints. Where transgression was clear, the warden imposed
swift justice. Where uncertainty remained, he was bound to morning, morning
being mercy.

On the Third Tenet. The
undertow represents the pull of one’s own temperament, which the Order
cautioned against. In short, the warden who killed from appetite and the warden
who spared from squeamishness had committed the same sin.

On the Fourth Tenet. A
fitness mandate for any sudden demand. The closing line reads as disdain for
weakness. Quite simply, it was better the watch stood empty than stood as an
open gate.

On the Fifth Tenet. The
warden who dies honorably joins the sacred dark, while the oathbreaker is given
the gloam in forfeiture of that communion. Sanctified in the watch, or
destroyed for leaving it.
The Prelate’s Letter

The second recovery is a letter
bearing the seal of the Duskwarden Prelate. It is addressed to a lovestruck
operative named Kahlil, who had evidently petitioned for a blessing of
marriage. The woman Kahlil wished to marry was a dawnwarden named Asia.

We present the letter in
Imperial Common in as literal a translation as the lexicon allows.
Kahlil,
paras.html: Kahlil,

paras.text:
I am glad you came to me. That you’ve
written so beautifully of this dawnwarden speaks a great deal of your heart and
the turmoil within it. Know that my own hand carries the same love for you, the
same wish for your life to be lived to its fullest extent.
paras.html: I am glad you came to me. That you’ve written so beautifully of this dawnwarden speaks a great deal of your heart and the turmoil within it. Know that my own hand carries the same love for you, the same wish for your life to be lived to its fullest extent.

paras.text:
You believe you are asking my leave to be
with Asia, but it is of her that I would urge you carefully reflect. You would
be a husband she never truly knows, because your oath requires silence. But in
time, she will learn of this locked door. And in time, you will pass her the
key.
paras.html: You believe you are asking my leave to be with Asia, but it is of her that I would urge you carefully reflect. You would be a husband she never truly knows, because your oath requires silence. But in time, she will learn of this locked door. And in time, you will pass her the key.

paras.text:
You will love her above all things, and one
night you will break her heart with the truth. And then, Kahlil, you will have
done to her what I am writing this letter to prevent. This light of hers you
love, the light that drew you up out of the dusk, will be dimmed. You will look
at her across your table or within your marital bed and understand too late
that in marrying the light you have only consumed it.
paras.html: You will love her above all things, and one night you will break her heart with the truth. And then, Kahlil, you will have done to her what I am writing this letter to prevent. This light of hers you love, the light that drew you up out of the dusk, will be dimmed. You will look at her across your table or within your marital bed and understand too late that in marrying the light you have only consumed it.

paras.text:
I encourage marriage within our family
because neither must keep a locked door. There is nothing in one that must be
hidden from the other, for they hold the same dusk between them. There is no
grief in them but the grief that is already unique to us. I bless such unions
gladly.
paras.html: I encourage marriage within our family because neither must keep a locked door. There is nothing in one that must be hidden from the other, for they hold the same dusk between them. There is no grief in them but the grief that is already unique to us. I bless such unions gladly.

paras.text:
Those who come to know what we are, and are
not bound by our oaths, seldom patron the morning. Kahlil, I write this because
I would not have you learn such truth the hard way. If you walk this path, I
cannot protect her.
paras.html: Those who come to know what we are, and are not bound by our oaths, seldom patron the morning. Kahlil, I write this because I would not have you learn such truth the hard way. If you walk this path, I cannot protect her.

paras.text:
So I withhold my blessing, and I do it as
your father would: against my own desire to see you happy. I know the ache you
carry, for I’ve walked this path before you. Find your completion within the
family, Kahlil, where I may be prodigal with my endowment and where no one need
pay for your happiness but you.

paras.text:
IN
CLOSING

Interestingly, the records
reveal a dawnwarden by the name of Kahlil’s beloved, noted for standing the
flame-watch. There is nothing to say what became of her, or if the two were
ever wed.

Moreover, the Committee cannot
establish that the Asia of the service record and the Asia of the Prelate’s
letter are the same woman. We can only conclude the irony that a warden of the
dusk, named for the poet of radiant love, should have set his heart on a woman
named after the land where dawn begins.

We had set out to compare two
organizations of the empire’s elite men and women, the one that kept the
morning and the one that kept the night. We now find that the comparison is not
as tidy as once thought, and that the peace was kept by hands we are only now
beginning to see. Sometimes at great price.

Archival
Committee, Citadel Repository of Letters, CP 1019
